# 12-Week Strength Programme
### Client Profile & Cycle-Aware Framework

---

## FOUNDATIONAL PLANNING LOGIC

**Cycle mapping from 2026-06-01:**

| Cycle | Menstruation (Flow Days 1–3) | Follicular / Ovulatory | Luteal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cycle 3 | ~May 29 – May 31 *(pre-programme)* | Jun 1–12 | Jun 13–25 |
| Cycle 4 | ~Jun 26 – Jun 28 | Jun 29 – Jul 10 | Jul 11–23 |
| Cycle 5 | ~Jul 24 – Jul 26 | Jul 27 – Aug 7 | Aug 8–20 |
| Cycle 6 | ~Aug 21 – Aug 23 | Aug 24 – Sep 4 | Sep 5–17 |

> **Note to trainer:** Dates are projections based on a 28-day cycle from May 1. Track actual cycle onset each month and shift the flow-restriction window accordingly. Build a 1-day buffer either side of projected flow days if her cycle varies by even 1–2 days.

**Three session archetypes used throughout:**

- **Type A – Full Strength:** Heavy compound work, progressive overload, Valsalva permitted. Used in follicular and mid-luteal windows.
- **Type B – Moderate Strength:** Moderate loads (65–75% 1RM), controlled breathing, no maximal bracing. Used in late luteal (days 24–28) as a natural deload lead-in.
- **Type C – Flow Day Session:** Low-intensity movement, no jumping, no heavy Valsalva, no loaded spinal compression. Restorative in nature. Attendance is *optional* — if she feels debilitated, full rest is equally valid. Never pressure attendance on flow days.

**Training frequency:** 3 sessions per week (Mon / Wed / Fri template — adjust to her schedule but maintain spacing).

---

## PROGRAMME PHASES

| Phase | Weeks | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 – Foundation | Weeks 1–4 | Movement quality, baseline strength, habit formation |
| Phase 2 – Accumulation | Weeks 5–8 | Volume and load increase, hypertrophy stimulus |
| Phase 3 – Intensification | Weeks 9–12 | Peak strength, heavier loading, performance testing |

---

---

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION (Weeks 1–4)
### *Goal: Establish movement patterns, build work capacity, learn RPE self-regulation*

**Loading parameters:** 3 sets across most exercises. RPE 6–7 (could do 3–4 more reps). Rest 90 seconds between sets for accessory work, 2 minutes for main lifts.

---

## WEEK 1 — June 1–7
**Cycle context:** Late follicular / approaching ovulation. Oestrogen rising — energy and recovery are typically excellent. Ideal week to establish baselines.

**Monday, June 1 — Type A: Lower Body Foundation**

Begin with a 5-minute general warm-up (light cycling or brisk walking) followed by dynamic mobility: leg swings, hip circles, bodyweight squats × 10, glute bridges × 10.

- *Goblet Squat:* 3 × 10 @ RPE 6. Focus on depth, neutral spine, and controlled descent. This is her primary squat pattern assessment.
- *Romanian Deadlift (dumbbells):* 3 × 10 @ RPE 6. Hinge pattern, soft knee, bar (or dumbbell) tracks close to the leg.
- *Walking Lunge:* 3 × 8 each leg, bodyweight. Assess balance and hip stability.
- *Glute Bridge:* 3 × 12, bodyweight or light barbell across hips. Full hip extension at top, 1-second pause.
- *Dead Bug:* 3 × 6 each side. Core stability, breathing pattern emphasis.
- Cool-down: 5 minutes static stretching — hip flexors, hamstrings, glutes.

**Wednesday, June 3 — Type A: Upper Body Foundation**

Warm-up: band pull-aparts × 15, shoulder circles, cat-cow × 10, scapular push-ups × 10.

- *Dumbbell Bench Press:* 3 × 10 @ RPE 6. Scapulae retracted and depressed, controlled eccentric.
- *Dumbbell Bent-Over Row:* 3 × 10 each side @ RPE 6. Neutral spine, elbow drives back, full range.
- *Seated Dumbbell Overhead Press:* 3 × 10 @ RPE 6. Rib cage down, no lumbar hyperextension.
- *Lat Pulldown (cable or machine):* 3 × 12 @ RPE 6. Initiate with scapular depression before elbow flexion.
- *Dumbbell Lateral Raise:* 3 × 12 @ RPE 5–6. Controlled, slight forward lean.
- *Plank:* 3 × 20–30 seconds. Neutral spine, breathe normally throughout.
- Cool-down: chest opener stretch, lat stretch, thoracic rotation.

**Friday, June 5 — Type A: Full Body / Pattern Integration**

Warm-up: 5 minutes light cardio, hip 90/90 mobility, thoracic rotations, band pull-aparts.

- *Trap Bar Deadlift (or conventional dumbbell deadlift if trap bar unavailable):* 3 × 8 @ RPE 6. Introduce the primary hinge pattern she will build on throughout the programme.
- *Dumbbell Split Squat:* 3 × 8 each leg @ RPE 6. Rear foot elevated optional if balance allows.
- *Cable Row (seated):* 3 × 10 @ RPE 6.
- *Push-Up (scaled to ability):* 3 × 8–12. Full range, body plank position.
- *Pallof Press:* 3 × 10 each side. Anti-rotation core stability.
- *Farmer's Carry:* 3 × 20 metres. Moderate load, tall posture, controlled breathing.
- Cool-down: full body stretch sequence, 5 minutes.

---

## WEEK 2 — June 8–14
**Cycle context:** Ovulation approximately June 12–13. Peak oestrogen and testosterone — research suggests this is often the highest-performance window of the cycle. Capitalise on this with a slight load increase.

Repeat the same session structure as Week 1 with the following progressions:

- Increase goblet squat and RDL load by one dumbbell increment (approximately 2–4 kg).
- Add 1 rep to walking lunges (3 × 9 each leg).
- Increase trap bar deadlift load by 5 kg.
- Increase dumbbell bench and row by one increment.
- Plank progresses to 3 × 35 seconds.
- Dead bug progresses to 3 × 8 each side.
- All other exercises maintain Week 1 loads and focus on improved technique quality.

**Trainer note:** Take informal 1RM estimates or 5RM tests this week on goblet squat and trap bar deadlift if you want baseline data for Phase 3 percentage work. Keep it conservative — RPE 8 maximum.

---

## WEEK 3 — June 15–21
**Cycle context:** Mid-luteal phase. Progesterone dominant. Many women report slightly reduced strength and increased perceived exertion. Maintain loads from Week 2 — do not push for new PRs. Focus on quality and consistency.

**Monday, June 15 — Type A: Lower Body**

Same exercise selection as Week 1/2. Loads held at Week 2 levels. Add a 4th set to goblet squat and RDL (4 × 10). This is a volume increase, not an intensity increase — appropriate for mid-luteal.

**Wednesday, June 17 — Type A: Upper Body**

Same exercise selection. Add a 4th set to bench press and row. Loads held.

**Friday, June 19 — Type A: Full Body**

Same exercise selection. Add a 4th set to trap bar deadlift. Introduce *Dumbbell Hip Thrust* (3 × 12) in place of glute bridge to begin progressing the posterior chain pattern.

---

## WEEK 4 — June 22–28
**Cycle context:** Late luteal (June 22–25) transitioning into menstruation (approximately June 26–28). This week requires the most careful session management of the entire programme.

**Monday, June 22 — Type B: Late Luteal Deload**

Reduce all loads by 10–15% from Week 3. Drop back to 3 sets. RPE cap at 6. This is intentional — her body is preparing for menstruation, and accumulated fatigue from the first three weeks warrants a reduction in stimulus. Frame this positively to the client: this is *planned recovery*, not regression.

- Goblet Squat: 3 × 8 @ RPE 5–6
- RDL: 3 × 8 @ RPE 5–6
- Dumbbell Hip Thrust: 3 × 10
- Seated Cable Row: 3 × 10
- Dumbbell Bench Press: 3 × 8
- Dead Bug: 3 × 8 each side
- Stretching emphasis: 10 minutes at end of session.

**Wednesday, June 24 — Type B: Late Luteal Deload**

Same approach. Prioritise movement quality and body awareness. Include 5 minutes of diaphragmatic breathing at the end of the session — this has evidence for reducing prostaglandin-related cramping when practised consistently in the days before menstruation.

- Trap Bar Deadlift: 3 × 6 @ RPE 5
- Split Squat: 3 × 6 each leg
- Lat Pulldown: 3 × 10
- Overhead Press: 3 × 8
- Pallof Press: 3 × 8 each side
- Farmer's Carry: 2 × 20 metres (lighter than previous weeks)

**Friday, June 26 — TYPE C: Flow Day Session (Optional)**

*Projected flow day 1. Attendance is entirely at the client's discretion.*

If she attends, this session is restorative and gentle. No Valsalva, no jumping, no heavy loading, no spinal compression under load.

- 10-minute walk on treadmill (comfortable pace, 0–2% incline)
- Supine hip circles: 2 × 10 each direction
- Cat-cow: 2 × 10
- Child's pose: 2 × 30 seconds
- Supine figure-4 stretch: 2 × 30 seconds each side
- Seated forward fold: 2 × 30 seconds
- Diaphragmatic breathing: 5 minutes
- *Optional:* Light resistance band work — clamshells 2 × 12, seated band abduction 2 × 12. These are low-load, low-intra-abdominal pressure movements that some women find helpful for pelvic circulation.

If she does not attend — that is the correct decision for her body that day. Log it as a planned rest day.

---

---

# PHASE 2 — ACCUMULATION (Weeks 5–8)
### *Goal: Increase training volume and load systematically, build hypertrophy base, introduce barbell work*

**Loading parameters:** 4 working sets on main lifts. RPE 7–8. Rest 2–2.5 minutes on main lifts, 90 seconds on accessories. Introduce barbell back squat and conventional barbell deadlift this phase (if movement quality from Phase 1 warrants it — use your clinical judgement).

---

## WEEK 5 — June 29 – July 5
**Cycle context:** Early follicular. Menstruation ending approximately June 28. Energy typically rebounds sharply in early follicular. This is an excellent week to introduce new stimuli and heavier loading.

**Monday, June 29 — Type A: Lower Body Strength**

Warm-up: 5 minutes bike, hip mobility circuit, goblet squat × 10 as activation.

- *Barbell Back Squat (or goblet squat if barbell not yet appropriate):* 4 × 6 @ RPE 7. Introduce Valsalva manoeuvre coaching here — proper bracing technique, not maximal straining. Controlled 3-second eccentric.
- *Romanian Deadlift (barbell):* 4 × 8 @ RPE 7.
- *Dumbbell Hip Thrust:* 3 × 12. Progress load from Phase 1.
- *Walking Lunge (dumbbells):* 3 × 10 each leg.
- *Copenhagen Plank:* 3 × 15–20 seconds each side. Adductor and core stability.
- *Pallof Press:* 3 × 10 each side.

**Wednesday, July 1 — Type A: Upper Body Strength**

- *Barbell Bench Press:* 4 × 6 @ RPE 7. Spot her appropriately. Controlled eccentric, full range.
- *Barbell Bent-Over Row:* 4 × 6 @ RPE 7. Overhand grip, hinge position, retract scapulae at top.
- *Seated Dumbbell Overhead Press:* 3 × 10 @ RPE 7.
- *Lat Pulldown:* 3 × 10 @ RPE 7.
- *Cable Face Pull:* 3 × 15. Shoulder health, rear delt and external rotator emphasis.
- *Tricep Pushdown:* 3 × 12.
- *Dumbbell Curl:* 3 × 12.

**Friday, July 3 — Type A: Full Body Power Endurance**

- *Trap Bar Deadlift:* 4 × 5 @ RPE 7–8. Heavier than Phase 1.
- *Bulgarian Split Squat (dumbbells):* 3 × 8 each leg @ RPE 7.
- *Cable Row:* 3 × 10.
- *Dumbbell Incline Press:* 3 × 10.
- *Farmer's Carry:* 4 × 25 metres. Increase load from Phase 1.
- *Ab Wheel Rollout (or TRX fallout):* 3 × 8. Progress from dead bug.

---

## WEEK 6 — July 6–12
**Cycle context:** Late follicular into ovulation (approximately July 10–11). Peak performance window. Push loads this week.

Maintain the same exercise selection as Week 5. Apply the following progressions:

- Barbell back squat: increase load 2.5–5 kg.
- Barbell bench press: increase load 2.5 kg.
- Barbell row: increase load 2.5–5 kg.
- Trap bar deadlift: increase load 5 kg.
- All accessory work: increase by one rep or one load increment where RPE allows.
- Add a 5th set to the back squat and trap bar deadlift on their respective days.

**Trainer note:** If she is responding well and technique is solid, this is a good week to establish a working 3RM on the back squat and trap bar deadlift. Keep it to RPE 8 — not a true max.

# Nutrition Plan: Cycle-Aware Fuelling
### Integrated with 12-Week Strength Programme

---

## FOUNDATIONAL PHILOSOPHY

This nutrition plan is built around two parallel goals: **supporting progressive strength adaptation** across all 12 weeks, and **actively mitigating the physiological drivers of primary dysmenorrhea** — elevated prostaglandins, systemic inflammation, iron depletion from heavy flow, and the hormonal fluctuations that affect energy, appetite, and recovery across the cycle. Every recommendation is evidence-informed and practical. Nothing here requires expensive supplements or radical dietary overhauls. The plan works with her existing eating habits as a starting point, layering in targeted adjustments phase by phase and cycle phase by cycle phase.

---

## SECTION 1: BASELINE NUTRITION TARGETS

### Calories

For a recreationally active 28-year-old woman in a strength programme, a rough maintenance starting point is calculated as follows. Adjust based on her actual stats when you have them.

**Estimated Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE):** Use her body weight in kg × 33–35 on training days, × 28–30 on rest days as a practical starting estimate. Refine after two weeks based on energy levels, performance, and body composition feedback.

The goal for this programme is **body recomposition with a strength bias** — not a caloric deficit. She should eat at or slightly above maintenance on training days, and at maintenance on rest days. Aggressive cutting during a strength programme will blunt adaptation and worsen dysmenorrhea symptoms, as low energy availability is independently associated with increased menstrual pain and cycle disruption.

> **Red flag to monitor:** If she reports persistent fatigue, worsening cramps, loss of menstrual regularity, or mood disturbance, consider whether energy availability has dropped too low. Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) can develop even in recreational athletes. Refer to her GP if concerned.

### Protein

**Target: 1.8–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight per day, every day of the cycle.**

Protein is non-negotiable and does not change with cycle phase. Adequate protein supports muscle protein synthesis, stabilises blood sugar (which worsens in late luteal for many women), and provides the amino acid substrate for neurotransmitter production — relevant because serotonin and dopamine fluctuations in the luteal phase contribute to mood changes and food cravings.

Distribute across **4 meals or eating occasions** of roughly equal protein content. Research consistently shows that spreading protein across the day is superior to front- or back-loading for muscle protein synthesis.

*Practical example for a 65 kg client:* 117–130 g protein per day, approximately 30–33 g per meal across four eating occasions.

**High-quality protein sources to emphasise:**
- Lean meats: chicken breast, turkey, lean beef mince, pork tenderloin
- Fish and seafood: salmon, sardines, mackerel, tuna, prawns *(these also deliver omega-3s — see below)*
- Eggs and egg whites
- Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, quark
- Legumes: lentils, chickpeas, black beans *(also high in iron and fibre — doubly valuable)*
- Tofu and tempeh
- Whey or plant-based protein powder as a convenient top-up, not a primary source

### Carbohydrates

**Target: 3–5 g per kg on training days, 2–3 g per kg on rest days.**

Carbohydrates are the primary fuel for strength training and are critical for maintaining training quality, particularly in the follicular and ovulatory phases when she is pushing hardest. Do not restrict carbohydrates — low-carbohydrate diets are associated with increased cortisol, disrupted sleep, and worsened menstrual symptoms.

**Carbohydrate timing:** Prioritise carbohydrates around training. A moderate-carbohydrate meal or snack 1–2 hours before training and a carbohydrate-containing meal within 1–2 hours after training will support performance and recovery.

**Preferred carbohydrate sources:**
- Oats, brown rice, quinoa, sweet potato, wholegrain bread and pasta
- Fruit: particularly berries (anti-inflammatory), bananas (potassium, pre-workout energy), and citrus (vitamin C enhances iron absorption — critical for her)
- Legumes (dual role: carbohydrate and protein)
- Root vegetables: carrots, parsnips, beetroot

### Fats

**Target: 1.0–1.2 g per kg per day.**

Dietary fat is essential for steroid hormone production — oestrogen and progesterone are synthesised from cholesterol. Women who drop dietary fat too low often experience cycle disruption. Fat also provides the vehicle for fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) that are relevant to her symptom management.

**Emphasise:**
- Omega-3 fatty acids: fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring), walnuts, flaxseed, chia seeds. *This is the single most evidence-supported dietary intervention for reducing dysmenorrhea severity — see Section 3.*
- Olive oil, avocado, avocado oil
- Nuts and seeds: almonds, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds
- Eggs (yolk included)

**Limit:**
- Omega-6-heavy vegetable oils (sunflower, corn, soybean oil in large quantities) — these compete with omega-3s for the same enzymatic pathways and can increase pro-inflammatory prostaglandin production
- Trans fats entirely

---

## SECTION 2: MICRONUTRIENTS OF CRITICAL IMPORTANCE

These are not optional extras. For a woman with severe primary dysmenorrhea and heavy flow, these micronutrients are directly implicated in symptom severity and training capacity.

---

### Iron

**Why it matters:** Heavy menstrual flow is the leading cause of iron deficiency in premenopausal women. Iron deficiency — even without frank anaemia — causes fatigue, reduced exercise capacity, impaired cognitive function, and worsened mood. Given that her flow days 1–3 are described as debilitating, iron status should be treated as a clinical priority.

**Recommendation:** Ask her GP to test serum ferritin (not just haemoglobin — ferritin is the storage form and depletes before anaemia develops). A ferritin below 30 µg/L is associated with fatigue and reduced performance even in the absence of anaemia. Optimal for athletic performance is generally considered 50–70 µg/L or above.

**Dietary iron targets:** Aim for 18 mg per day from food (the RDA for premenopausal women), with a practical target of 20–25 mg on the days immediately following menstruation to begin replenishing stores.

**Haem iron sources (most bioavailable — absorbed at 15–35%):**
- Beef, lamb, liver (liver is exceptionally rich — 6–7 mg per 100 g — but limit to once weekly due to vitamin A content)
- Chicken and turkey (dark meat higher than white)
- Sardines, oysters, mussels, clams

**Non-haem iron sources (absorbed at 2–20%, but still valuable):**
- Lentils (3.3 mg per 100 g cooked), chickpeas, kidney beans
- Tofu (2.7 mg per 100 g)
- Spinach, kale, fortified cereals
- Pumpkin seeds, cashews, quinoa

**Critical pairing rule — vitamin C with non-haem iron:** Consuming vitamin C alongside non-haem iron sources increases absorption by up to 3-fold. Practical examples: lemon juice squeezed over lentils, orange juice with fortified cereal, bell peppers in a bean stew, tomatoes with tofu.

**Critical avoidance rule — calcium and tannins inhibit iron absorption:** Do not consume dairy, tea, or coffee within 1 hour of an iron-rich meal. This is particularly important in the post-menstrual recovery window (days 4–7 of her cycle).

---

### Magnesium

**Why it matters:** Magnesium is arguably the most evidence-supported micronutrient for dysmenorrhea. It works through multiple mechanisms: it inhibits prostaglandin synthesis, relaxes uterine smooth muscle, reduces systemic inflammation, supports sleep quality, and modulates the HPA stress axis. Deficiency is extremely common — estimated at 50–80% of Western populations — and is worsened by stress, heavy exercise, and high sugar intake.

**Dietary target:** 320 mg per day (RDA for women 19–30), with a practical aim of 350–400 mg given her training load.

**Best dietary sources:**
- Dark leafy greens: spinach (78 mg per 100 g cooked), Swiss chard
- Pumpkin seeds (156 mg per 28 g — exceptionally rich)
- Dark chocolate 70%+ (64 mg per 28 g — also provides iron and is a psychologically satisfying inclusion)
- Almonds, cashews, Brazil nuts
- Black beans, edamame, lentils
- Avocado (58 mg per medium avocado)
- Banana (32 mg — also useful pre-workout)
- Whole grains: brown rice, oats, quinoa
- Salmon, mackerel

**Supplementation consideration:** If dietary intake is consistently below target, a magnesium glycinate or magnesium citrate supplement of 200–300 mg taken in the evening is well-tolerated and has the added benefit of improving sleep quality. Magnesium oxide is poorly absorbed and not recommended. Advise her to discuss with her GP before starting any supplement.

---

### Omega-3 Fatty Acids (EPA and DHA)

**Why it matters:** This is the most robustly evidenced dietary intervention for primary dysmenorrhea. Prostaglandins — specifically PGE2 and PGF2α — are the primary drivers of uterine cramping. Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) compete with arachidonic acid (an omega-6 fatty acid) for the same COX enzymes that produce prostaglandins. Higher omega-3 intake shifts prostaglandin production toward less inflammatory, less vasoconstrictive forms, directly reducing cramping severity. Multiple randomised controlled trials have demonstrated significant reductions in dysmenorrhea pain scores with omega-3 supplementation.

**Dietary target:** Aim for 2–3 portions of oily fish per week (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring, anchovies). Each portion provides approximately 1.5–2.5 g of combined EPA and DHA.

**Supplementation:** If she does not eat oily fish regularly, an omega-3 supplement providing 1–2 g of combined EPA and DHA per day is appropriate. Fish oil or algae-based omega-3 (suitable for vegetarians/vegans) are both effective. Advise her to take it with a meal containing fat for best absorption and to discuss with her GP.

**Practical inclusion ideas:** Tinned sardines on wholegrain toast, smoked mackerel in salads, salmon fillet twice weekly, anchovies in pasta sauces or on pizza.

---

### Vitamin D

**Why it matters:** Vitamin D receptors are present in uterine tissue. Low vitamin D is independently associated with increased dysmenorrhea severity, and supplementation trials have shown reductions in pain scores. It also supports immune function, mood regulation, and muscle recovery — all relevant to her programme.

**Recommendation:** Test serum 25(OH)D via her GP. Optimal range for athletic performance and hormonal health is generally considered 75–125 nmol/L. In the UK and many northern latitudes, supplementation of 1,000–2,000 IU per day is appropriate for most people from October to April at minimum, and year-round for many individuals.

**Dietary sources** (limited but worth including): Oily fish, egg yolks, fortified dairy and plant milks, mushrooms exposed to UV light.

---

### Calcium

**Why it matters:** Calcium has a direct role in smooth muscle contraction regulation. Low calcium intake is associated with increased uterine cramping. Several trials have shown that calcium supplementation reduces dysmenorrhea pain, particularly when combined with vitamin D (which is required for calcium absorption).

**Dietary target:** 1,000 mg per day.

**Best sources:** Dairy (milk, yoghurt, cheese), fortified plant milks, tinned fish with bones (sardines, salmon), tofu set with calcium sulphate, kale, broccoli, almonds, white beans.

**Note on timing:** As mentioned above, avoid calcium-rich foods within 1 hour of iron-rich meals to prevent absorption competition.

---

### Zinc

**Why it matters:** Zinc has anti-inflammatory and prostaglandin-inhibiting properties. It is also lost through heavy menstrual flow. Low zinc is associated with increased menstrual pain.

**Dietary sources:** Red meat, shellfish (oysters are exceptionally rich), pumpkin seeds, hemp seeds, legumes, nuts, whole grains.

---

### B Vitamins (particularly B1 — Thiamine, and B6)

**Why it matters:** Thiamine (B1) supplementation has shown significant reductions in dysmenorrhea severity in clinical trials. B6 supports progesterone production and serotonin synthesis, relevant to luteal phase mood and PMS symptoms.

**Dietary sources:** Whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, lean meat, fish, eggs, leafy greens. A good-quality B-complex supplement is a reasonable consideration — discuss with GP.

---

## SECTION 3: CYCLE-PHASE NUTRITION ADJUSTMENTS

The following adjustments layer on top of the baseline targets above. They are not dramatic shifts — they are targeted tweaks that align with the hormonal and physiological reality of each cycle phase.

---

### MENSTRUATION — Days 1–3 (Flow Days)
*Approximately: Jun 26–28, Jul 24–26, Aug 21–23*

**Physiological context:** Prostaglandins are at their highest. Iron loss is occurring. Inflammation is elevated. Energy may be low. Appetite can be suppressed or erratic. The goal of nutrition on these days is to reduce inflammatory load, support iron replacement, and provide comfort without exacerbating symptoms.

**Key priorities:**

**Anti-inflammatory eating:** Maximise omega-3 intake. Include oily fish, walnuts, flaxseed, or chia seeds on these days specifically. Minimise processed foods, refined sugar, and alcohol — all of which amplify the inflammatory prostaglandin response and worsen cramping.

**Iron-rich foods from day 1:** Begin iron replenishment immediately. Even though she is still losing blood, starting iron-rich foods on day 1 rather than waiting until flow ends gives her a head start. Prioritise haem iron sources (lean red meat, sardines) alongside vitamin C.

**Magnesium-rich foods:** Dark chocolate, pumpkin seeds, leafy greens, avocado. These support smooth muscle relaxation and may reduce cramping intensity.

**Hydration:** Increase water intake to 2.5–3 litres per day. Dehydration worsens cramping. Herbal teas — particularly ginger tea and chamomile tea — have mild anti-inflammatory and antispasmodic properties and are a comforting, evidence-adjacent choice. Ginger specifically has been shown in small trials to reduce dysmenorrhea pain comparably to ibuprofen.

**Reduce:** Caffeine (vasoconstriction can worsen cramping — if she is caffeine-dependent, reduce rather than eliminate to avoid withdrawal headaches), alcohol, salty processed foods (increase bloating and water retention), and high-sugar foods (spike inflammation and worsen mood instability).

**Sodium:** Moderate sodium intake to reduce bloating and water retention, which can worsen pelvic discomfort.

**Sample flow day eating pattern:**

- *Breakfast:* Porridge with chia seeds, banana, and a handful of walnuts. Ginger tea.
- *Lunch:* Lentil and spinach soup with a squeeze of lemon juice (vitamin C + iron). Wholegrain bread.
- *Snack:* Greek yoghurt with berries and a square of dark chocolate.
- *Dinner:* Grilled salmon with roasted sweet potato and steamed broccoli. Water with lemon.
- *Evening:* Chamomile tea. Magnesium glycinate supplement if prescribed.

**Calorie note:** If appetite is suppressed on flow days, do not force full calorie targets. Prioritise protein and micronutrient density over total volume. Liquid nutrition (smoothies, soups) can be easier to consume when nausea or discomfort is present.

---

### EARLY FOLLICULAR — Days 4–7
*The recovery window immediately post-menstruation*

**Physiological context:** Oestrogen begins rising. Energy returns. Iron stores are at their lowest point of the cycle. This is the most important window for iron replenishment.

**Key priorities:**

**Iron replenishment is the number one nutritional priority this week.** Aim for at least one iron-rich meal per day, always paired with vitamin C. Avoid tea and coffee within 1 hour of these meals.

**Rebuild energy availability:** Return to full calorie targets. Appetite typically increases naturally — lean into this with nutrient-dense whole foods rather than processed convenience foods.

**Protein:** Maintain 1.8–2.0 g/kg. Muscle protein synthesis rates begin to increase as oestrogen rises — adequate protein ensures she can capitalise on this.

**Sample early follicular day:**

- *Breakfast:* Scrambled eggs (3) with spinach and tomatoes on wholegrain toast. Orange juice (vitamin C to enhance iron from eggs and spinach).
- *Lunch:* Beef and vegetable stir-fry with brown rice. Bell peppers (vitamin C).
- *Snack:* Apple with almond butter. Handful of pumpkin seeds.
- *Dinner:* Lentil dahl with quinoa and roasted cauliflower.
- *Post-training:* Whey protein shake with milk, banana, and a tablespoon of peanut butter.

---

### LATE FOLLICULAR AND OVULATORY — Days 8–14
*Peak performance window*

**Physiological context:** Oestrogen peaks. Testosterone briefly spikes around ovulation. Energy, strength, and recovery are typically at their best. This is the phase where she will be training hardest.

**Key priorities:**

**Maximise training fuel:** Increase carbohydrate intake toward the higher end of the target range (4–5 g/kg on training days). Pre-training meals should be carbohydrate-rich and moderate in protein. Post-training meals should combine protein and carbohydrates for recovery.

**Pre-training meal (1.5–2 hours before session):** 40–60 g carbohydrates, 20–25 g protein, low fat and fibre to avoid GI discomfort. Example: chicken and rice, Greek yoghurt with banana and oats, or a turkey sandwich on wholegrain bread.

**Post-training meal (within 1–2 hours):** 40–60 g carbohydrates, 30–40 g protein. Example: salmon with sweet potato and vegetables, or a protein shake with oats and fruit followed by a full meal within 2 hours.

**Hydration:** 2–2.5 litres per day. Increase on training days.

**Note on oestrogen and protein synthesis:** Research suggests that oestrogen may enhance muscle protein synthesis and reduce muscle damage from exercise. This is the phase to push training volume and load — her nutrition should fully support this.

**Sample late follicular training day:**

- *Breakfast:* Greek yoghurt (200 g) with granola, mixed berries, and honey. Coffee (fine this phase).
- *Pre-training snack (1.5 hrs before):* Banana and a rice cake with peanut butter.
- *Post-training:* Whey protein shake with oat milk and a banana.
- *Lunch:* Grilled chicken breast, quinoa, roasted vegetables, olive oil dressing.
- *Dinner:* Beef stir-fry with brown rice, broccoli, and sesame seeds.
- *Evening snack:* Cottage cheese with pineapple (casein protein for overnight recovery).

---

### EARLY-TO-MID LUTEAL — Days 15–21
*Progesterone dominant, maintain training quality*

**Physiological context:** Progesterone rises. Basal metabolic rate increases slightly (approximately 100–300 kcal per day above follicular phase baseline — this is real and measurable). Appetite increases. Cravings for carbohydrates and fats are common and are physiologically driven, not a lack of willpower. Blood sugar regulation becomes slightly less efficient. Core temperature is elevated by approximately 0.3–0.5°C.

**Key priorities:**

**Honour the increased energy need:** Add approximately 150–250 kcal to daily intake in the luteal phase, primarily from complex carbohydrates and healthy fats. This is not overeating — it is meeting a genuine physiological demand. Restricting calories in the luteal phase tends to worsen cravings, mood, and training performance.

**Blood sugar stability:** Prioritise low-glycaemic carbohydrates and avoid large refined sugar loads, which cause blood sugar spikes and crashes that amplify luteal phase mood instability and fatigue. Pair carbohydrates with protein and fat at every meal.

**Manage cravings intelligently:** Dark chocolate (magnesium + satisfaction), nut butter on fruit, roasted sweet potato with cinnamon, and oat-based snacks are all nutrient-dense ways to meet carbohydrate and fat cravings without derailing nutrition quality.

**Tryptophan-rich foods:** Serotonin production decreases in the luteal phase for many women. Tryptophan is the dietary precursor to serotonin. Sources include turkey, eggs, dairy, oats, bananas, nuts, and seeds. Including these regularly may support mood stability.

**Continue omega-3 emphasis:** Prostaglandins begin building in the luteal phase in preparation for menstruation. Maintaining high omega-3 intake throughout the luteal phase — not just during flow — is important for blunting the prostaglandin surge at menstruation onset.

**Sample mid-luteal day:**

- *Breakfast:* Oat porridge with almond butter, banana, and cinnamon. Boiled egg on the side.
- *Lunch:* Turkey and avocado wrap in a wholegrain tortilla with salad. Apple.
- *Snack:* Handful of mixed nuts and a square of dark chocolate.
- *Dinner:* Mackerel fillet with roasted sweet potato, green beans, and olive oil.
- *Evening:* Warm milk with honey (tryptophan + comfort). Magnesium supplement.

*Pre-menstrual window, deload nutrition alignment*

**Physiological context:** Both oestrogen and progesterone drop sharply. This hormonal withdrawal is the trigger for PMS symptoms — bloating, breast tenderness, mood changes, fatigue, food cravings, and the beginning of prostaglandin accumulation. This phase aligns with her Type B deload sessions.

**Key priorities:**

**Anti-inflammatory preparation:** This is the most important window for dietary prostaglandin management. The dietary choices she makes in days 22–28 directly influence the severity of her flow day cramping. Maximise omega-3 intake, minimise omega-6 and processed food intake, eliminate alcohol, and reduce caffeine.

**Reduce sodium and refined carbohydrates:** Both worsen bloating and water retention, which are already elevated due to hormonal shifts.

**Maintain magnesium:** Magnesium deficiency is most symptomatic in this phase. Prioritise magnesium-rich foods daily and consider the evening supplement.

**Vitamin B6:** Eggs, chicken, fish, bananas, potatoes, and fortified cereals. B6 supports progesterone production and serotonin synthesis — both relevant to late luteal symptoms.

**Calcium:** Ensure she is hitting 1,000 mg per day. Calcium has been shown to reduce PMS symptoms including mood changes, bloating, and cramping.

**Avoid:** Alcohol (worsens inflammation, disrupts sleep, depletes B vitamins and magnesium), caffeine in excess (worsens breast tenderness and anxiety), high-sugar foods, and ultra-processed foods.

**Hydration:** Counterintuitively, drinking more water reduces water retention by signalling to the kidneys that fluid is not scarce. Target 2.5–3 litres per day.

# Cardio Programming: Aerobic Base Development
### Cycle-Aware Integration with 12-Week Strength Programme

---

## FOUNDATIONAL PHILOSOPHY

Building an aerobic base for a strength-focused client requires a clear understanding of what "aerobic base" actually means physiologically, and why the method of building it matters enormously when layered onto an existing strength programme with cycle-phase constraints.

The aerobic base — sometimes called the aerobic foundation or Zone 2 capacity — refers to the efficiency of the oxidative energy system: the mitochondrial density of muscle tissue, cardiac stroke volume, capillary density, and the ability to sustain moderate-intensity effort primarily through fat oxidation without accumulating lactate. A well-developed aerobic base improves recovery between strength sets, accelerates post-session recovery, supports cardiovascular health, and enhances overall work capacity. It also has meaningful benefits for hormonal health, stress regulation, and sleep quality — all directly relevant to dysmenorrhea management.

The critical principle governing this plan is **polarisation**: the vast majority of cardio work (approximately 80%) will be performed at genuinely low intensity — Zone 1 and Zone 2 — and a small proportion (approximately 20%) at moderate-to-hard intensity, but only during the appropriate cycle windows and never on flow days. There will be **no high-intensity interval training (HIIT), no plyometric cardio, and no maximal-effort work on flow days**, in full compliance with her GP clearance. Outside flow days she is fully cleared, and the programme will use that window intelligently.

The second governing principle is **interference management**. Concurrent training — combining strength and endurance work — carries a well-documented risk of blunting strength adaptations if cardio volume, intensity, or timing is poorly managed. The strategies used here to minimise interference are: separating cardio and strength sessions by at least 6 hours where possible, performing cardio after strength on combined days rather than before, keeping the majority of cardio at low intensity (which produces minimal interference with strength signalling), and managing total weekly training volume carefully so that recovery is never compromised.

---

## HEART RATE ZONES — ESTABLISHING HER TRAINING ZONES

Before prescribing specific intensities, establish her individual heart rate zones. The most practical field method without laboratory testing is as follows.

**Estimated Maximum Heart Rate:** 220 minus age = 192 bpm. This is a population estimate — actual HRmax may vary by ±10–15 bpm. If she has access to a maximal effort test (a graded treadmill test or a hard 3-minute all-out effort on a bike), use that number instead.

**Note on luteal phase heart rate:** Resting heart rate increases by approximately 2–5 bpm in the luteal phase, and heart rate at any given workload is slightly elevated compared to the follicular phase. This means that if she is training to heart rate targets, she should use **perceived exertion (RPE) as the primary guide in the luteal phase**, with heart rate as secondary information. A Zone 2 effort should feel like Zone 2 — not look like Zone 2 on a watch when her resting HR is already elevated.

| Zone | Name | % HRmax | Approx BPM (HRmax 192) | RPE (1–10) | Feel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zone 1 | Active Recovery | 50–60% | 96–115 | 2–3 | Easy conversation, barely breathing harder |
| Zone 2 | Aerobic Base | 60–70% | 115–134 | 3–4 | Full sentences, slightly aware of breathing |
| Zone 3 | Aerobic Tempo | 70–80% | 134–154 | 5–6 | Short sentences, comfortably uncomfortable |
| Zone 4 | Threshold | 80–90% | 154–173 | 7–8 | A few words only, sustained effort |
| Zone 5 | VO2 Max | 90–100% | 173–192 | 9–10 | Cannot speak, maximal |

**For this programme:** Zone 1 and Zone 2 are the primary training zones throughout. Zone 3 is introduced in Phase 2 during follicular and ovulatory windows only. Zone 4 is introduced briefly in Phase 3 during the peak follicular and ovulatory window only. Zone 5 is never prescribed — it constitutes high-intensity work and is not appropriate given her condition and the interference risk with strength training.

## CARDIO MODALITY SELECTION

The following modalities are approved for this programme. Selection should be guided by her preferences, equipment availability, and cycle phase.

**Primary modalities (suitable all cycle phases including flow days at low intensity):**
- **Cycling (stationary or outdoor):** Excellent for aerobic base development. Low impact, no spinal loading, easily regulated by power or heart rate. Strongly preferred on flow days as it is seated, low-impact, and does not involve Valsalva or jumping.
- **Walking (flat to moderate incline):** The most accessible and underrated aerobic tool. Brisk walking at 5–6.5 km/h on a treadmill or outdoors is genuine Zone 1–2 work. Incline walking (8–12%) elevates heart rate into Zone 2 without impact. Ideal for flow days and deload weeks.
- **Swimming or pool walking:** Excellent low-impact option. The hydrostatic pressure of water may actually reduce pelvic discomfort on flow days for some women. If she has access and is comfortable, this is a valuable flow-day option.
- **Elliptical trainer:** Low impact, full body, easily regulated. Good alternative to cycling when variety is needed.

**Secondary modalities (follicular and ovulatory phases only, not on flow days):**
- **Rowing machine:** Moderate impact on the lower back under fatigue — use with good technique. Excellent full-body aerobic stimulus. Avoid on flow days due to the hip flexion and intra-abdominal pressure involved in the drive phase.
- **Light jogging / run-walk intervals:** Introduced in Phase 2 follicular window only, if she expresses interest in running. Begin with run-walk protocols (e.g., 1 minute running, 2 minutes walking) to manage impact load alongside strength training.

**Modalities excluded from this programme:**
- Jump rope, plyometric cardio, aerobics classes with jumping, sprint intervals — all excluded on flow days per GP clearance. Outside flow days these are technically cleared but are not prescribed here as they conflict with the aerobic base goal (which is best built at low intensity) and the interference management strategy.

## TRAINER BRIEFING

Before applying these revisions, a few important clinical and programming notes.

Pushing intensity in Phase 2 is absolutely appropriate given positive client feedback — this is exactly the kind of real-world adjustment good programming requires. However, three guardrails must remain non-negotiable regardless of how strong she feels.

**Guardrail one — cycle phase respect:** Intensity increases are applied in the follicular and ovulatory windows. The late luteal and flow day protocols do not change. Feeling strong in the follicular phase is partly a function of peak oestrogen and testosterone — this is the biology working as intended. Capitalise on it in those windows. Do not use it as justification to push through the luteal deload.

**Guardrail two — technique before load:** Every load increase must be preceded by a technique check. As loads increase into the 80–85% 1RM range, form breakdown risk increases significantly. If you see bar path deviation, knee cave, lumbar flexion under load, or loss of bracing, the load does not go up that session regardless of how she feels.

**Guardrail three — fatigue monitoring:** Feeling strong is a green light to push. Feeling strong but sleeping poorly, having elevated resting heart rate, or reporting unusual soreness is a yellow light — push conservatively or hold. Implement a simple daily readiness check: ask her to rate sleep quality, energy, and motivation out of 10 each training day. If the combined score is below 15/30, reduce planned loads by 10% and reassess mid-session.

## REVISED LOADING PARAMETERS FOR PHASE 2

The original Phase 2 used RPE 7–8 across 4 working sets. The revised Phase 2 applies the following upgrades:

**Main compound lifts (squat, deadlift, bench, row, overhead press):**
- Working sets increase to RPE 8–8.5 on primary lift days
- Top sets introduced: one heavier set above the working weight at RPE 8.5–9 before back-off sets
- Back-off sets added: 2–3 sets at 85–90% of top set weight for volume accumulation
- Set structure moves from straight sets to a **top set plus back-off** model, which allows both intensity and volume to increase simultaneously without simply grinding through fatigue

**Accessory lifts:**
- RPE increases to 7.5–8
- Rep ranges tighten slightly (from 10–12 to 8–10) to allow heavier loading
- Volume maintained or slightly increased

**Rest periods:**
- Main lifts: 3 minutes between all working sets
- Accessories: 90–120 seconds
- After top sets: 3.5–4 minutes before first back-off set

**Progression model within Phase 2:**
- Week 5: Establish top set loads, conservative RPE 8
- Week 6: Increase top set loads, push to RPE 8.5 on primary lifts
- Week 7: Maintain Week 6 loads, increase back-off set volume (add one set)
- Week 8: Deload as planned — non-negotiable

**Percentage estimates for reference** (based on projected 1RMs from Phase 1 testing):
- Top sets: approximately 82–87% 1RM
- Back-off sets: approximately 72–78% 1RM
- These are guides — RPE governs, not percentages

# Important Clinical Hold — HIIT Prescription Requires Clarification

---

Before writing a single HIIT session for this client, I need to flag a direct conflict with her medical clearance that requires your decision as the trainer, and potentially a return conversation with her GP.

---

## THE CONFLICT

Her GP clearance states explicitly:

> **"On flow days: NO high-intensity exercise."**

HIIT — by definition — is high-intensity exercise. A standing weekly HIIT day on a fixed day of the week will, across a 12-week programme with a 28-day cycle, land on or immediately adjacent to a flow day **multiple times**. This is not a edge case. It is a mathematical certainty.

**Mapping it out precisely:**

| Cycle | Projected Flow Days 1–3 | Day of Week |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle 4 | June 26–28 | Friday – Sunday |
| Cycle 5 | July 24–26 | Thursday – Saturday |
| Cycle 6 | August 21–23 | Friday – Sunday |

Any fixed HIIT day — Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday — will conflict with at least one flow window across the 12 weeks. A Thursday HIIT day conflicts directly with Cycle 5 flow. A Friday conflicts with Cycles 4 and 6. There is no fixed day of the week that is safe across all three cycles.

Beyond the GP restriction, there are two additional clinical concerns worth raising with her:

**Concern one — prostaglandins and high-intensity exercise:** During menstruation, circulating prostaglandins are at their peak. High-intensity exercise acutely elevates inflammatory cytokines and cortisol. In women with primary dysmenorrhea, this combination can significantly worsen cramping, nausea, and systemic symptoms during and after the session. This is not universal — some women tolerate it — but for a client whose flow days are described as *debilitating*, the risk of a severe symptom flare is real and should not be dismissed.

**Concern two — Valsalva and intra-abdominal pressure:** Many HIIT formats involve burpees, jump squats, kettlebell swings, battle ropes, and similar movements that generate significant intra-abdominal pressure. Her GP has specifically excluded heavy Valsalva on flow days. Several common HIIT exercises would violate this restriction even if the intensity restriction were somehow navigated.

---

## YOUR OPTIONS AS THE TRAINER

I can build this HIIT programming in three different ways depending on how you want to handle the conflict. Tell me which approach you want and I will write the full plan.

---

### Option A — Cycle-Phased HIIT (Recommended)
**What it is:** HIIT is programmed as a floating session that is scheduled each month based on her actual cycle. It is placed in the follicular or ovulatory window only — never within 2 days of projected flow onset, never during flow. In practice this means she gets 2–3 HIIT sessions per cycle, which across 12 weeks is 6–9 sessions total. Each session is fully compliant with her GP clearance.

**What you gain:** Full HIIT stimulus during the windows when she is physiologically best equipped to handle it and recover from it. Oestrogen in the follicular phase enhances carbohydrate metabolism and high-intensity performance. She will likely hit better numbers and recover faster from HIIT in this window than she would mid-luteal anyway.

**What you give up:** A fixed weekly HIIT day. She and you need to plan each month's schedule in advance based on her cycle tracking.

**Best for:** A client who is engaged with her cycle tracking, motivated, and understands the rationale. Given that she is already working within a cycle-aware programme, this is likely her.

---

### Option B — Modified Metabolic Conditioning (No True HIIT)
**What it is:** Replace HIIT with a metabolic conditioning format that achieves similar cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes without reaching the intensity threshold that triggers the GP restriction. This uses circuit-style resistance training, kettlebell complexes, and tempo work at Zone 3–4 rather than Zone 5. It can be scheduled on a fixed weekly day because the intensity ceiling keeps it below the high-intensity threshold on flow days — it simply becomes a gentler version of itself during that window.

**What you gain:** A fixed weekly session that never needs to be moved. Simpler scheduling. Still delivers meaningful metabolic conditioning and caloric expenditure.

**What you give up:** True HIIT stimulus — the supramaximal efforts, the VO2 max ceiling work, the acute EPOC effect of genuine high-intensity intervals. This is a meaningful compromise.

**Best for:** A client who wants simplicity, or one whose primary goal is body composition rather than peak cardiovascular performance.

---

### Option C — Full HIIT Plan with Explicit Flow Day Substitution Protocol
**What it is:** A complete HIIT programme written for every week, with a clearly documented substitution protocol for any week where the scheduled HIIT day falls within the flow window. The substitution is a pre-written alternative session — not a rest day, not an improvised decision, but a planned lower-intensity metabolic session that delivers what is safely possible on that day.

**What you gain:** A complete written plan for every scenario. Nothing is left to in-the-moment decision making. The client always knows what she is doing.

**What you give up:** Slightly more complexity in the programme document. Requires the client to track her cycle and communicate onset to you promptly.

**Best for:** A trainer who wants everything documented and a client who appreciates having a clear plan for every eventuality.

---

### Option D — Return to GP First
**What it is:** Before adding HIIT, you go back to her GP with a specific question: *"The client wants to add weekly HIIT sessions. Given her severe primary dysmenorrhea, are you comfortable clearing her for high-intensity exercise outside of flow days, and do you have any specific restrictions around the perimenstrual window — the 1–2 days before flow onset?"*

**Why this matters:** The current clearance covers the situation as originally described. Adding a new training modality — particularly one that is explicitly in the category of what was restricted — warrants a specific clearance rather than an assumption that "outside flow days" covers everything. A 2-minute phone call or a brief letter to the GP protects you, protects her, and may yield useful clinical information about her specific presentation.

**Best for:** Any situation where you have any doubt. This is always the right answer when a client's medical history intersects with a new training stimulus.

---

**Option A as the primary structure, with Option C's substitution protocol built in, after an Option D check-in with her GP.**

In practical terms: go back to the GP with the specific HIIT question, get explicit clearance for high-intensity work outside the flow window, then build a cycle-phased HIIT plan with documented flow-day substitutions for every week where the conflict arises.

## THE CONFLICT IS IDENTICAL

Her GP clearance states:

> **"On flow days: NO jumping."**

Plyometrics are, by definition, jumping. Every foundational plyometric movement — box jumps, broad jumps, depth jumps, bounding, hurdle hops, jump squats, lateral bounds, single-leg hops — is explicitly in the category of what her GP has restricted on flow days.

The fixed-day scheduling problem is the same as HIIT and the maths is the same:

| Cycle | Projected Flow Days 1–3 | Day of Week |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle 4 | June 26–28 | Friday – Sunday |
| Cycle 5 | July 24–26 | Thursday – Saturday |
| Cycle 6 | August 21–23 | Friday – Sunday |

There is no fixed day of the week that clears all three flow windows across 12 weeks. A standing plyometric day will collide with flow days. This is not a risk — it is a certainty.

---

## THERE IS AN ADDITIONAL CONCERN SPECIFIC TO PLYOMETRICS

Beyond the GP restriction, there is a biomechanical risk factor for this client that does not apply to HIIT in the same way, and it is worth you knowing about it before programming any jumping work regardless of cycle phase.

**ACL injury risk and the menstrual cycle:**

This is one of the most robustly evidenced areas in female sports medicine. Multiple prospective studies — including large-scale research on female athletes across football, basketball, and handball — have demonstrated that ACL injury risk is significantly elevated in the pre-ovulatory phase when oestrogen peaks, and to a lesser extent in the late luteal phase when both oestrogen and progesterone are fluctuating rapidly. The proposed mechanisms include:

- Oestrogen receptors in ligamentous tissue respond to peak oestrogen by reducing ligament stiffness and increasing laxity — the same joint laxity that makes women more flexible also makes their ligaments more compliant under load
- Neuromuscular control of the knee — specifically the ability to co-contract the hamstrings to protect the ACL during landing — is measurably reduced at peak oestrogen
- Progesterone in the luteal phase has a partially protective effect on ligament stiffness, but the rapid withdrawal of both hormones in late luteal creates a window of altered neuromuscular control

**What this means practically:**

It does not mean she should not do plyometrics. It means plyometric programming for female clients requires cycle-aware landing mechanics coaching, progressive load introduction, and awareness that her injury risk profile is not constant across the month. Jumping onto a box on day 12 of her cycle carries a different neuromuscular risk profile than jumping on day 20. This is not a reason to avoid plyometrics — it is a reason to programme them intelligently, which is exactly what a good trainer does.

**The practical mitigation:**

- Prioritise landing mechanics before any loaded or high-intensity plyometric work
- Include hamstring activation and neuromuscular warm-up before every plyometric session regardless of cycle phase
- Be more conservative with volume and intensity in the late follicular and ovulatory window specifically — counterintuitive given that this is her peak performance window, but the ACL data is clear enough to warrant caution with high-impact landing tasks
- The mid-follicular window — approximately days 5–9 of her cycle — is actually the sweet spot for plyometric work: oestrogen is rising but has not yet peaked, progesterone is low, neuromuscular control is good, and energy is high

# 1RM Testing at End of Phase 3 — Clinical and Programming Assessment

---

## SHORT ANSWER

**Yes — with specific modifications, and not on all lifts equally.**

A 1RM test at the end of a 12-week programme is a legitimate and motivating goal. It is also entirely achievable for this client. However, the standard 1RM testing protocol used for general population strength athletes needs three specific adjustments for her, and one of those adjustments is cycle-dependent in a way that could meaningfully affect both her safety and the validity of the result.

Here is the full picture.

---

## CONCERN ONE — CYCLE TIMING IS EVERYTHING FOR A VALID 1RM

A 1RM test is a maximal voluntary contraction effort. The number she produces on testing day is not purely a function of her trained strength — it is a function of her trained strength expressed through the hormonal, neurological, and psychological state she is in on that specific day. Test her on day 2 of her flow and you will get a number that underrepresents her true capacity by a meaningful margin. Test her in the mid-follicular window and you will get her best honest number.

**Projected cycle state in Week 12 (August 17–23):**

Based on her 28-day cycle from May 1:

- Cycle 6 menstruation begins approximately **August 21**
- Week 12 runs approximately **August 17–23**
- This means the **first half of Week 12 is late luteal** and the **second half is flow**

This is not ideal for a 1RM test. Late luteal is characterised by progesterone withdrawal, elevated perceived exertion, potential mood disruption, and reduced neuromuscular efficiency. Flow days are explicitly restricted from heavy Valsalva by her GP.

**The solution is not to abandon the 1RM test. It is to move it.**

---

## THE TIMING RECOMMENDATION

Rather than testing in Week 12 as originally planned, shift the peak testing day to **Week 11, mid-follicular equivalent** — or more precisely, to the best available follicular window in the final two weeks of the programme.

**Revised end-of-programme testing window:**

Looking at her cycle, the optimal testing window falls in **early-to-mid Week 11**, approximately **August 10–14**. At this point she is in the mid-follicular phase of Cycle 6 — oestrogen rising, energy high, neuromuscular efficiency at its best, and well clear of both the preceding flow days and the approaching late luteal window.

**Revised programme endpoint structure:**

| Week | Dates | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Week 10 | Aug 3–9 | Peak loading — heaviest training week, final strength stimulus |
| Week 11 | Aug 10–16 | **1RM Testing Week** — mid-follicular, optimal window |
| Week 12 | Aug 17–23 | Transition week — late luteal, active recovery, programme review, next phase planning |

This structure gives her a proper peaking stimulus in Week 10, a 3–5 day taper into testing, and uses Week 12 as a meaningful wind-down rather than forcing a maximal test into a hormonally compromised window.

**Communicate this to her clearly:** The reason her test is in Week 11 rather than Week 12 is not because Week 12 is a failure or an afterthought. It is because you have deliberately engineered the programme so that her peak expression of strength coincides with her peak physiological readiness. This is sophisticated programming, not a compromise.

---

## CONCERN TWO — WHICH LIFTS TO TEST

Not all lifts are equally appropriate for a 1RM test in this context. The decision should be based on three criteria: technical maturity of the movement, spinal loading profile, and intra-abdominal pressure demands.

**Recommended for 1RM testing:**

**Trap Bar Deadlift** — First choice for a maximal lower body pull test. The trap bar's neutral grip and more upright torso position reduces shear force on the lumbar spine compared to conventional deadlift, making it a safer maximal effort for a client who has been training for 12 weeks rather than years. She has been building this lift since Week 1. Technical maturity is high. Intra-abdominal pressure at maximal effort is significant but manageable with proper bracing technique that she will have developed across the programme.

**Barbell Bench Press** — Appropriate for 1RM testing. Upper body maximal efforts generate substantially less intra-abdominal pressure than lower body compound lifts. The bench press is the most technically stable of the pressing movements and the one she has the most exposure to. Requires a competent spotter — non-negotiable on a true 1RM attempt.

**Barbell Back Squat** — Appropriate with caveats. She has been squatting since Phase 1 and the movement quality should be well established by Week 11. The back squat generates the highest intra-abdominal pressure of the three recommended lifts. Ensure her bracing technique is solid before attempting a true maximum. If there is any doubt about technical readiness for a maximal squat, substitute a 3RM instead — see below.

**Not recommended for true 1RM testing:**

**Conventional Barbell Deadlift** — If she has been using the trap bar as her primary deadlift pattern, do not switch to conventional for a 1RM test. Testing a movement pattern that is less technically mature than the training pattern produces an invalid result and increases injury risk. Test what she has trained.

**Overhead Press** — The overhead press is not an appropriate 1RM test lift for most recreational clients. Maximal overhead pressing requires exceptional thoracic mobility, shoulder stability, and lumbar control under load. A failed 1RM overhead press has a poor bail-out option. Test a 3RM or 5RM here instead.

**Romanian Deadlift, Hip Thrust, Split Squat** — These are assistance lifts in this programme, not primary strength indicators. Do not test 1RMs on assistance movements.

---

## CONCERN THREE — THE VALSALVA QUESTION ON FLOW DAYS

This concern is resolved by the timing shift above — testing in Week 11 mid-follicular means she is well clear of flow days. However, document this clearly in your session notes: **if her cycle runs early and flow begins before or during the testing window, the 1RM test is postponed, not cancelled.** Have a pre-agreed postponement protocol so this decision is never made under pressure on the day.

**Postponement protocol:** If flow begins within 3 days of the scheduled test date, postpone by 5–7 days into the following follicular window. The strength she has built does not disappear in a week. A slightly delayed test on a good day is worth infinitely more than a compromised test on a bad day.

### Test Day Session Structure

**Order of testing:** Squat first, bench second, deadlift third. This follows the convention of powerlifting competition and has a logical fatigue rationale — the squat is the most technically demanding and benefits most from full freshness, the deadlift is the most systemically fatiguing and should come last.

Allow **full recovery between lifts** — minimum 15–20 minutes between the last attempt on one lift and the warm-up for the next. This is a long session. Budget 2.5–3 hours including warm-up and rest periods.

---

**LIFT ONE — BARBELL BACK SQUAT**

*Total time including warm-up: approximately 45–55 minutes*

**Warm-up protocol:**

The warm-up for a 1RM test is more structured than a regular training warm-up. Each set serves a specific purpose — progressively loading the nervous system, reinforcing the movement pattern, and building confidence without accumulating fatigue.

- 5 minutes general warm-up: light bike or walk, get the body temperature up
- Dynamic mobility: leg swings × 10 each direction, hip circles × 10, bodyweight squat × 10 with 3-second pause at bottom, glute bridge × 15
- Empty bar × 8 — focus on technique, breathing, bar position
- 40% estimated 1RM × 5 — still easy, moving with intent
- 55% × 3 — starting to feel like a squat
- 65% × 2 — controlled, confident
- 75% × 1 — this should feel solid and fast
- 82% × 1 — heavier, still should not be a grind
- 88% × 1 — this is the last warm-up set. Rest 3 minutes after this.

**Attempt selection:**

The art of 1RM testing is attempt selection. Too conservative and she leaves weight on the bar. Too aggressive and she misses attempts, accumulates fatigue, and loses confidence. The following framework works well:

- **Attempt 1:** 92–93% of estimated 1RM. This should be a confident, clean lift. If it is a grind, stop here — her 1RM is approximately 97% of this weight and you can calculate it. If it moves well, proceed.
- **Attempt 2:** 97–98% of estimated 1RM. This is the target 1RM or just below. Rest 4–5 minutes after Attempt 1.
- **Attempt 3:** 100–103% of estimated 1RM — only if Attempt 2 was successful and moved with reasonable speed. Rest 5 minutes after Attempt 2. This is the PR attempt.

**Maximum three attempts per lift.** Failed attempts count toward the three. Do not add a fourth attempt — the fatigue and psychological cost of a failed lift make a fourth attempt almost always counterproductive.

**Rest between attempts:** 4 minutes minimum, 5 minutes preferred. Use a timer. Do not rush.

**Spotting protocol for the squat:** Two spotters if available — one each side of the bar. If only one spotter (you), stand directly behind her, hands ready at her hips, do not touch the bar unless she is in genuine danger of going down. Verbal cues during the lift: "drive," "up," "push" — short, clear, timed to the sticking point.

**What a good 1RM squat looks like:** Bar path is vertical, depth is at or below parallel, knees track over toes throughout, lumbar spine maintains neutral through the entire lift, she stands up under control. A lift where the chest caves, the knees collapse inward, or the lumbar rounds significantly is a technical failure regardless of whether she stands up with it. Make the call clearly and consistently.

---

**15-minute rest between squat and bench warm-up. She should sit, hydrate, eat a small carbohydrate snack if needed — a banana or a few rice cakes — and mentally reset.**

---

**LIFT TWO — BARBELL BENCH PRESS**

*Total time including warm-up: approximately 40–50 minutes*

**Warm-up protocol:**

- Shoulder mobility: arm circles, band pull-aparts × 20, shoulder CARs × 5 each side
- Empty bar × 10
- 40% × 5
- 55% × 3
- 65% × 2
- 75% × 1
- 82% × 1
- 88% × 1 — rest 3 minutes

**Attempt selection:** Same framework as squat — 92%, then 97–98%, then 100–103% if warranted.

**Rest between attempts:** 4–5 minutes.

**Spotting protocol for bench:** Stand directly behind the bar, hands under but not touching the bar. Liftoff assistance if she wants it — agree the liftoff protocol before the attempt. During the lift, watch for bar path deviation and be ready to take the bar immediately if she calls for it or if the bar stops moving. Do not touch the bar unless necessary — a touched lift is not a valid 1RM.

**What a good 1RM bench looks like:** Scapulae retracted and depressed throughout, bar touches lower chest with control, drive is explosive and bar path is consistent, feet remain on the floor, glutes remain on the bench, no excessive arch that removes range of motion. A lift where the bar bounces off the chest, the spotter assists the concentric, or the feet leave the floor is not valid.

---

**15–20 minute rest between bench and deadlift warm-up. This is the longest rest of the day — the deadlift is the most systemically demanding lift and she needs to be as recovered as possible. Hydrate, eat if needed, walk around gently.**

---

**LIFT THREE — TRAP BAR DEADLIFT**

*Total time including warm-up: approximately 45–55 minutes*

**Warm-up protocol:**

- Hip hinge with dowel × 10, single-leg RDL bodyweight × 8 each side, glute bridge × 15, dead bug × 6 each side
- 40% × 5
- 55% × 3
- 65% × 2
- 75% × 1
- 82% × 1
- 88% × 1 — rest 4 minutes. The deadlift warm-up requires longer rest than squat and bench because the systemic fatigue from the earlier lifts is accumulating.

**Attempt selection:** Same framework — 92%, then 97–98%, then 100–103%.

**Rest between attempts:** 5 minutes minimum. After a heavy squat and bench session, her systemic fatigue is real. Do not rush the deadlift attempts.

**No spotter needed for deadlift** — the lift has a natural bail-out (drop the bar). Ensure the platform is clear and the collars are secure.

**What a good 1RM trap bar deadlift looks like:** Back set before the pull, lats engaged, hips drive the movement, bar path is vertical, lockout is achieved with glutes not lumbar hyperextension, controlled lowering or a safe drop. A lift where the lower back rounds significantly under load, the hips shoot up before the shoulders, or she cannot achieve lockout is not valid.

## POST-TESTING PROTOCOL

**Immediately after the final lift:**

- Do not rush out of the gym. 10 minutes of gentle walking and light stretching.
- Hydrate — she will have been in the gym for 2.5–3 hours.
- Eat within 30–45 minutes — a full meal with protein and carbohydrates. This is not the day to be precious about nutrition timing. She has just done something genuinely hard and her body needs fuel.

**Document everything:**

For each lift, record:
- All warm-up set loads
- All three attempt loads
- Whether each attempt was successful
- RPE rating for each successful attempt
- Any technical observations
- Her subjective experience — how she felt, what surprised her, what she wants to improve

This documentation serves two purposes: it validates the result for her (seeing the progression from warm-up to 1RM is motivating) and it gives you precise data for programming the next training block.

## CALCULATING ESTIMATED 1RM FROM TRAINING DATA

If for any reason the test needs to be postponed — cycle runs early, she is unwell, life intervenes — you can calculate a reliable estimated 1RM from her training data using the Epley formula:

**Estimated 1RM = Weight lifted × (1 + reps ÷ 30)**

Example: If she completed 3 reps at 80 kg on the squat in Week 10:
80 × (1 + 3 ÷ 30) = 80 × 1.1 = **88 kg estimated 1RM**

# Full 12-Week Programme Summary
### Cycle-Aware Strength, Cardio, Nutrition & Power Development
#### Client: 28F, Recreational Lifter, Severe Primary Dysmenorrhea
#### Programme Start: June 1, 2026

---

## MASTER REFERENCE DOCUMENT

This summary consolidates every component discussed across all previous conversations into a single navigable reference. It is designed to be used session by session, week by week, with the detailed session notes from the individual programme documents available as the expanded reference when needed.

---

## CLIENT PROFILE & NON-NEGOTIABLES

**Age:** 28
**Training history:** Recreational lifter
**Medical condition:** Severe primary dysmenorrhea
**GP clearance:** Full clearance for exercise with three permanent restrictions on flow days 1–3:
- No high-intensity exercise
- No heavy Valsalva / maximal intra-abdominal pressure
- No jumping

**Cycle data:**
- Last period started: May 1, 2026
- Cycle length: 28 days, regular
- Flow days 1–3: debilitating
- Outside flow window: fully cleared for all training

**Programme goals:**
1. Build progressive strength across squat, deadlift, and bench press
2. Develop aerobic base
3. Metabolic conditioning (cycle-phased, pending GP confirmation of HIIT clearance)
4. Athletic power development (cycle-phased, pending GP confirmation and physiotherapy landing mechanics screen)
5. Manage and reduce dysmenorrhea symptoms through training and nutrition
6. Establish sustainable long-term training habits

---

## CYCLE PROJECTION MAP — FULL 12 WEEKS

| Cycle | Flow Days 1–3 | Early Follicular | Late Follicular / Ovulation | Early-Mid Luteal | Late Luteal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cycle 4 | Jun 26–28 | Jun 29 – Jul 2 | Jul 3–12 | Jul 13–20 | Jul 21–25 |
| Cycle 5 | Jul 24–26 | Jul 27–30 | Jul 31 – Aug 9 | Aug 10–17 | Aug 18–20 |
| Cycle 6 | Aug 21–23 | Aug 24–27 | Aug 28 onwards | — | — |

**Buffer rule:** Apply a 1-day buffer either side of all projected flow dates. If her cycle varies, shift all session type designations accordingly. She must communicate cycle onset to you promptly — ideally on day 1 — so the current week's sessions can be confirmed or adjusted.

---

## SESSION TYPE DEFINITIONS

| Type | Name | When Used | Key Parameters |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Full Strength | Follicular, ovulatory, early-mid luteal | Heavy compounds, Valsalva permitted, RPE 7–9 |
| B | Moderate Strength | Late luteal (days 22–28) | 10–15% load reduction, RPE cap 6, 3 sets |
| C | Flow Day | Days 1–3 | No jumping, no Valsalva, no spinal loading, restorative, attendance optional |

---

## DAILY READINESS CHECK

Ask her to rate three metrics out of 10 at the start of every training session:
- Sleep quality last night
- Energy level right now
- Motivation to train

**Score 24–30:** Proceed as planned. Green light.
**Score 15–23:** Proceed with slight load reduction (5–10%). Monitor mid-session.
**Score below 15:** Reduce planned loads by 10–15%, cap RPE at 7, consider converting Type A to Type B. Investigate cause — poor sleep, life stress, under-eating, or approaching flow window.

---

## TRAINING WEEK TEMPLATE

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Strength Session 1 |
| Tuesday | Cardio Session 1 |
| Wednesday | Strength Session 2 |
| Thursday | Cardio Session 2 |
| Friday | Strength Session 3 |

| Sunday | Full rest |

Adjust days to her schedule but maintain the spacing principle: strength sessions separated by at least one day, cardio after strength on combined days never before.

# PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION
## Weeks 1–4 | June 1–28
### Goal: Movement quality, baseline strength, habit formation, aerobic habit establishment

## WEEK 1 — June 1–7
**Cycle phase:** Late follicular. Oestrogen rising. Excellent energy and recovery. Ideal week to establish baselines.

**Nutrition focus:** Full baseline targets. Iron-rich foods daily. Omega-3 emphasis begins.
